title: What story fits each expression?
description: Two expressions, eight x plus three y and fifteen x minus two x, are matched to everyday stories about buying fruit and selling pencils. The question is open ended and any sensible story with the right quantities works.
teaching_notes: One idea: a number before a letter can be a price or a count, and a minus sign can be something taken away. Watch for stories that do not use the numbers in the expression.

video_script.why: A learner uses the method of reading a formula back into a situation: each term of the expression is matched to a quantity in the story, as the matchstick formula was matched to the matchstick steps.
video_script.substitution: The method of reading what each term of a formula counts, with the cost of fruit and the sale of pencils in place of the matchsticks.
video_script.anchor: a fruit seller and a packet of pencils, each matched to an expression
video_script.payoff_line: Each expression now has its own story

final_answer.value: (a) x mangoes at 8 rupees and y bananas at 3 rupees (b) a packet of 15 pencils at x rupees with 2 unsold, giving 13x rupees
final_answer.spoken: one model story for each expression; many other stories also work

hold_back: Answer: (a) x mangoes at 8 rupees and y bananas at 3 rupees (b) a packet of 15 pencils at x rupees with 2 unsold, giving 13x rupees
never_show: the full model stories before their steps
maths_rules: (a) mangoes at 8 rupees each, bananas at 3 rupees each; x mangoes and y bananas cost 8x + 3y rupees
(b) a packet of 15 pencils at x rupees each is worth 15x; 2 unsold take away 2x; 15x - 2x = 13x rupees
video_script.design: One idea: match each term of the expression to one quantity in a short story. Assumes the example of reading a formula back into a situation. The two expressions stay on the stage.
open_questions: The question is open ended; the video gives one model story for each expression, as in the worklist, and says that other stories work.

<bookmark mark='s1b'/>A fruit seller sells mangoes at eight rupees each and bananas at three rupees each.

<bookmark mark='s3b'/>A packet has fifteen pencils, and each pencil costs x rupees. The full packet is worth fifteen x rupees.

beats.on_screen: Step 5, check: x = 2, y = 3 gives 16 + 9 = 25 and 8x + 3y = 25 ; x = 2 gives 30 − 4 = 26 and 13x = 26

marks.s5a: x as 2 and y as 3 are chosen
marks.s5c: 2 mangoes and 3 bananas are paid for

narration: <bookmark mark='s5a'/>Fifth, check with x as two and y as three. <bookmark mark='s5c'/>Two mangoes cost sixteen and three bananas cost nine, which is twenty five rupees. The expression gives twenty five as well.
<bookmark mark='s5b'/>For the pencils, the packet is worth thirty and two unsold pencils take away four, leaving twenty six. Thirteen times two is twenty six.

beats.on_screen: Answer: (a) x mangoes at 8 rupees and y bananas at 3 rupees (b) a packet of 15 pencils at x rupees with 2 unsold, giving 13x rupees
